text.title: A Mother
text.author: James Joyce
text.description: Mrs. Kearney, a determined woman of refined accomplishments, becomes embroiled in a conflict with the organizers of a concert series when payment for her daughter Kathleen's services as accompanist is threatened. Her insistence on contractual rights leads to a dramatic confrontation that ends with her withdrawal from the event.

holohan.name: Mr. Holohan
holohan.description: Assistant secretary of the Eire Abu Society who organizes a series of concerts. He has a game leg and is called 'Hoppy Holohan' by friends. Despite his efforts, he is ultimately ineffectual in managing the concert arrangements and becomes the target of Mrs. Kearney's anger.
textMentions: Mr Holohan, assistant secretary of the _Eire Abu_ Society
He had a game leg and for this his friends called him Hoppy Holohan
Mr Holohan came into the dressing-room every few minutes with reports from the box-office
holohan.context: Member of the Eire Abu Society during the Irish Revival period

data.occupation: Assistant secretary of Eire Abu Society

mrs-kearney.name: Mrs. Kearney
mrs-kearney.description: A woman of refined accomplishments and strong will who becomes the central figure in a conflict over payment for her daughter's services. Formerly Miss Devlin, she married Mr. Kearney out of spite and has devoted herself to her family's advancement. She is determined, organized, and uncompromising in her pursuit of contractual rights.
textMentions: Miss Devlin had become Mrs Kearney out of spite
Mrs Kearney who arranged everything
Mrs Kearney was well content at this
mrs-kearney.context: Dublin woman of the Irish Revival period, educated in convent, married to bootmaker

kathleen-kearney.name: Miss Kathleen Kearney
kathleen-kearney.description: Daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Kearney, educated in music and French. She becomes the accompanist for the concert series and is caught between her mother's demands and the committee's expectations. She is musically talented and known in nationalist circles.
textMentions: her daughter should be the accompanist at a series of four grand concerts
Miss Kathleen Kearney began to be heard often on people's lips
Kathleen gathered in her skirt and said: _"Now, Mr Bell,"_
kathleen-kearney.context: Young woman of Dublin during Irish Revival, educated in music and French

mr-kearney.name: Mr. Kearney
mr-kearney.description: A bootmaker on Ormond Quay, much older than his wife. He is sober, thrifty, and pious, attending mass regularly. He serves as a stabilizing force in the family and supports his wife's efforts, though he remains largely passive during the concert crisis.
textMentions: Mr Kearney, who was a bootmaker on Ormond Quay
His conversation, which was serious, took place at intervals in his great brown beard
he went to the altar every first Friday
mr-kearney.context: Dublin bootmaker, married to refined woman, father of two daughters

data.physicalDescription: Much older than wife, great brown beard, coughs

fitzpatrick.name: Mr. Fitzpatrick
fitzpatrick.description: Secretary of the Eire Abu Society. A small man with a white vacant face who seems indifferent to the problems of the concert organization. He chews the programme and appears unable to resolve the payment dispute with Mrs. Kearney.
textMentions: the secretary of the Society, Mr Fitzpatrick
He was a little man, with a white vacant face
he chewed one end of it into a moist pulp
fitzpatrick.context: Secretary of Eire Abu Society during concert series

data.physicalDescription: Little man with white vacant face, wears soft brown hat carelessly, flat accent

duggan.name: Mr. Duggan
duggan.description: A bass singer who has risen from humble origins as a hall porter's son to become a first-rate artiste. He has appeared in grand opera and performed at the Queen's Theatre. He is unassuming, speaks little, and abstains from alcohol for his voice.
textMentions: The bass, Mr Duggan, was a slender young man with a scattered black moustache
he had sung prolonged bass notes in the resounding hall
he never drank anything stronger than milk for his voice's sake
duggan.context: Professional bass singer in Dublin during Irish Revival

data.physicalDescription: Slender young man with scattered black moustache

bell.name: Mr. Bell
bell.description: A second tenor and first item on the concert programme. He is fair-haired, small, and extremely nervous and jealous of other tenors. He competes annually at the Feis Ceoil and has won a bronze medal. He covers his nervousness with ebullient friendliness.
textMentions: Mr Bell, the second tenor, was a fair-haired little man
He was extremely nervous and extremely jealous of other tenors
It was his humour to have people know what an ordeal a concert was to him
bell.context: Professional tenor singer in Dublin, competitor at Feis Ceoil

madam-glynn.name: Madam Glynn
madam-glynn.description: A soprano from London who performs at the concert. She is unknown to the Dublin audience and sings in an old-fashioned style with poor technique. Her performance of 'Killarney' is poorly received, particularly by the cheaper seats.
textMentions: An unknown solitary woman with a pale face walked through the room
Someone said that she was Madam Glynn, the soprano
Madam Glynn from London
madam-glynn.context: Professional soprano from London performing in Dublin

data.physicalDescription: Pale face, faded blue dress on meagre body, startled gaze

miss-healy.name: Miss Healy
miss-healy.description: A contralto singer and friend of Kathleen Kearney. She is caught between loyalty to Kathleen and the other artistes. She eventually agrees to play accompaniments for the second part of the concert when Mrs. Kearney refuses.
textMentions: Miss Healy, the contralto
Kathleen stood chatting to one of her Nationalist friends, Miss Healy
Miss Healy had kindly consented to play one or two accompaniments
miss-healy.context: Professional contralto singer and nationalist friend of Kathleen

data.physicalDescription: Young woman with warm body and fragrance

first-tenor.name: First Tenor
first-tenor.description: A well-dressed, stout, and complacent tenor who performs successfully at the concert. He brings an air of opulence to the dressing room and performs well in the first part.
textMentions: The first tenor and the baritone arrived together
They were both well dressed, stout and complacent
The first tenor and the contralto, however, brought down the house

data.physicalDescription: Well dressed, stout, complacent, wears gold chain across waist

baritone.name: Baritone
baritone.description: A well-dressed, stout, and complacent baritone who performs at the concert. He is sympathetic to Mrs. Kearney's position but wishes to remain at peace with all parties.
textMentions: The first tenor and the baritone arrived together
They were both well dressed, stout and complacent
The baritone was asked what did he think of Mrs Kearney's conduct

o-madden-burke.name: Mr. O'Madden Burke
o-madden-burke.description: A suave, elderly man who is widely respected. He balances his imposing body on a large silk umbrella and is known for his magniloquent western name. He attends the concert and condemns Mrs. Kearney's conduct, suggesting she should receive no payment.
textMentions: Mr O'Madden Burke, who had found out the room by instinct
He was a suave, elderly man who balanced his imposing body, when at rest, upon a large silk umbrella
Mr O'Madden Burke said it was the most scandalous exhibition he had ever witnessed
o-madden-burke.context: Respected Dublin figure, critic and observer of cultural events

data.physicalDescription: Suave, elderly man with imposing body, uses large silk umbrella

hendrick.name: Mr. Hendrick
hendrick.description: A grey-haired journalist from the Freeman newspaper who comes to report on the concert but must leave early to cover an American priest's lecture at the Mansion House. He is plausible in manner and finds Miss Healy's company appealing.
textMentions: The _Freeman_ man had come in to say that he could not wait for the concert
He was a grey-haired man, with a plausible voice and careful manners
Thank you very much, Mr Hendrick
hendrick.context: Journalist for Freeman newspaper in Dublin

data.physicalDescription: Grey-haired man with plausible voice and careful manners, holds extinguished cigar

miss-beirne.name: Miss Beirne
miss-beirne.description: A little woman who is a member of the Committee. She is brought out by a steward to speak with Mrs. Kearney. She is trustful and enthusiastic but becomes melancholy when looking at the rainy street.

data.physicalDescription: Little woman with oldish face, twisted features

miss-devlin.name: Miss Devlin

e01.description: Mr. Holohan, assistant secretary of the Eire Abu Society, walks up and down Dublin for nearly a month with his hands and pockets full of dirty pieces of paper, arranging about the series of concerts. He has a game leg and is called 'Hoppy Holohan' by friends.

e02.description: Miss Devlin had become Mrs. Kearney out of spite. She had been educated in a high-class convent where she learned French and music. As she was naturally pale and unbending in manner she made few friends at school.

e03.description: Miss Devlin marries Mr. Kearney, a bootmaker on Ormond Quay, when she draws near the limit of marriageable age and her friends begin to loosen their tongues about her.

e04.description: Mr. Kearney proves to be a model father and husband. He is sober, thrifty, and pious. He pays a small sum every week into a society to ensure dowries for both daughters. He sends Kathleen to a good convent and pays her fees at the Academy.

e05.description: Every year in the month of July, Mrs. Kearney finds occasion to say to some friend that her good man is packing them off to Skerries, Howth, or Greystones for a few weeks.

e06.description: When the Irish Revival begins to be appreciable, Mrs. Kearney determines to take advantage of her daughter's name and brings an Irish teacher to the house.

e07.description: Kathleen and her sister send Irish picture postcards to their friends, and these friends send back other Irish picture postcards. On special Sundays, when Mr. Kearney goes with his family to the pro-cathedral, a little crowd of people assemble after mass at the corner of Cathedral Street.

e08.description: The name of Miss Kathleen Kearney begins to be heard often on people's lips. People say that she is very clever at music and a very nice girl, and moreover, that she is a believer in the language movement.

e09.description: Mr. Holohan comes to Mrs. Kearney and proposes that her daughter should be the accompanist at a series of four grand concerts which his Society is going to give in the Antient Concert Rooms. Mrs. Kearney brings him into the drawing-room, makes him sit down, and brings out the decanter and the silver biscuit-barrel.

e10.description: A contract is drawn up by which Kathleen is to receive eight guineas for her services as accompanist at the four grand concerts.

e11.description: Mrs. Kearney helps Mr. Holohan with the details of the concert enterprise. She advises and dissuades on matters of bills and programme. She knows what artistes should go into capitals and what should go into small type. She knows that the first tenor would not like to come on after Mr. Meade's comic turn.

e12.description: Mrs. Kearney buys some lovely blush-pink charmeuse in Brown Thomas's to let into the front of Kathleen's dress. She takes a dozen two-shilling tickets for the final concert and sends them to friends who could not be trusted to come otherwise.

e13.description: When Mrs. Kearney arrives with her daughter at the Antient Concert Rooms on Wednesday night, she does not like the look of things. A few young men wearing bright blue badges stand idle in the vestibule. None of them wear evening dress. A quick glance through the open door shows her the cause of the stewards' idleness.

e14.description: In the dressing-room behind the stage, Mrs. Kearney is introduced to Mr. Fitzpatrick, the secretary of the Society. He is a little man with a white vacant face. He wears his soft brown hat carelessly on the side of his head and has a flat accent. He holds a programme in his hand and chews one end of it into a moist pulp.

e15.description: The concert on Wednesday night proceeds with few people in the hall. Mr. Fitzpatrick comes in and says 'Well now, ladies and gentlemen. I suppose we'd better open the ball.' Mrs. Kearney rewards his very flat final syllable with a quick stare of contempt. The concert expires shortly before ten, and everyone goes home quickly.

e16.description: The concert on Thursday night is better attended, but Mrs. Kearney sees at once that the house is filled with paper. The audience behaves indecorously, as if the concert were an informal dress rehearsal. Mr. Fitzpatrick seems to enjoy himself, standing at the edge of the screen and exchanging laughs with friends in the balcony.

e17.description: In the course of the Thursday evening, Mrs. Kearney learns that the Friday concert is to be abandoned and that the Committee is going to move heaven and earth to secure a bumper house on Saturday night. She seeks out Mr. Holohan and asks if it is true.

e18.description: Mrs. Kearney tells Mr. Holohan that the contract was for four concerts and that her daughter should receive the sum originally stipulated for, whether the society gives the four concerts or not. Mr. Holohan advises her to speak to Mr. Fitzpatrick. Mrs. Kearney says she doesn't know anything about Mr. Fitzpatrick and intends to see that the contract is carried out.

e19.description: Little boys are sent out into the principal streets of Dublin early on Friday morning with bundles of handbills. Special puffs appear in all the evening papers, reminding the music-loving public of the treat which is in store for it on the following evening.

e20.description: Mrs. Kearney tells her husband part of her suspicions about the concert arrangements. He listens carefully and suggests that perhaps it would be better if he went with her on Saturday night. She agrees, respecting her husband in the same way as she respects the General Post Office, as something large, secure and fixed.

e21.description: The night of the grand concert comes. Mrs. Kearney, with her husband and daughter, arrives at the Antient Concert Rooms three-quarters of an hour before the time at which the concert is to begin. By ill luck it is a rainy evening. Mrs. Kearney places her daughter's clothes and music in charge of her husband.

e22.description: Mrs. Kearney goes all over the building looking for Mr. Holohan or Mr. Fitzpatrick. She cannot find either. She asks the stewards if any member of the Committee is in the hall. After a great deal of trouble, a steward brings out Miss Beirne, to whom Mrs. Kearney explains that she wants to see one of the secretaries.

e23.description: The bass, Mr. Duggan, arrives at the dressing-room. He is a slender young man with a scattered black moustache. He is the son of a hall porter and has raised himself to become a first-rate artiste. He has appeared in grand opera and once performed the part of the king in Maritana at the Queen's Theatre.

e24.description: Mr. Bell, the second tenor, arrives. He is a fair-haired little man who competes every year for prizes at the Feis Ceoil. On his fourth trial he had been awarded a bronze medal. He is extremely nervous and extremely jealous of other tenors. When he sees Mr. Duggan, he asks 'Are you in it too?' and they shake hands.

e25.description: An unknown solitary woman with a pale face walks through the dressing-room. The women follow with keen eyes the faded blue dress stretched upon a meagre body. Someone says that she is Madam Glynn, the soprano. Kathleen asks Miss Healy who the unknown woman is. Mr. Holohan says she is Madam Glynn from London.

e26.description: The first tenor and the baritone arrive together. They are both well dressed, stout and complacent and they bring a breath of opulence among the company. Mrs. Kearney brings her daughter over to them and talks to them amiably.

e27.description: Mrs. Kearney excuses herself and goes out after Mr. Holohan. She asks him when her daughter is going to be paid. Mr. Holohan says that Mr. Fitzpatrick has charge of that. Mrs. Kearney says she doesn't know anything about Mr. Fitzpatrick and that her daughter has signed a contract for eight guineas and will have to be paid.

e28.description: Mr. Hendrick, a grey-haired journalist from the Freeman newspaper, comes into the dressing-room. He says he cannot wait for the concert as he has to report a lecture by an American priest at the Mansion House. He is old enough to suspect one reason for Miss Healy's politeness but young enough in spirit to turn the moment to account. Mr. O'Madden Burke, a suave elderly man, is also present.

e29.description: While Mr. Holohan is entertaining the Freeman man, Mrs. Kearney speaks so animatedly to her husband that he has to ask her to lower her voice. The conversation in the dressing-room becomes strained. Mr. Bell stands ready with his music but the accompanist makes no sign. From the hall come sounds of encouragement, clapping and stamping of feet.

e30.description: Mr. Fitzpatrick bursts into the room, followed by Mr. Holohan, who is panting. The clapping and stamping in the hall are punctuated by whistling. Mr. Fitzpatrick holds a few banknotes in his hand. He counts out four into Mrs. Kearney's hand and says she will get the other half at the interval. Mrs. Kearney says 'This is four shillings short.'

e31.description: Kathleen gathers in her skirt and says 'Now, Mr Bell' to the first item. The singer and the accompanist go out together. The noise in the hall dies away. There is a pause of a few seconds and then the piano is heard.

e32.description: The first part of the concert is very successful except for Madam Glynn's item. The poor lady sings Killarney in a bodiless gasping voice with all the old-fashioned mannerisms of intonation and pronunciation. She looks as if she has been resurrected from an old stage-wardrobe and the cheaper parts of the hall make fun of her high wailing notes.

e33.description: The first tenor and the contralto bring down the house. Kathleen plays a selection of Irish airs which is generously applauded. The first part closes with a stirring patriotic recitation delivered by a young lady who arranges amateur theatricals. It is deservedly applauded.

e34.description: During the interval, in one corner of the dressing-room are Mr. Holohan, Mr. Fitzpatrick, Miss Beirne, two stewards, the baritone, the bass, and Mr. O'Madden Burke. Mr. O'Madden Burke says it was the most scandalous exhibition he has ever witnessed. He says Miss Kathleen Kearney's musical career was ended in Dublin after that. The baritone is asked what he thinks of Mrs. Kearney's conduct but does not like to say anything.

e35.description: In another corner of the dressing-room are Mrs. Kearney and her husband, Mr. Bell, Miss Healy, and the young lady who had to recite the patriotic piece. Mrs. Kearney says that the Committee has treated her scandalously. She has spared neither trouble nor expense and this is how she is repaid. She appeals to Mr. Bell and Miss Healy for support.

e36.description: As soon as the first part is ended, Mr. Fitzpatrick and Mr. Holohan go over to Mrs. Kearney and tell her that the other four guineas will be paid after the Committee meeting on the following Tuesday. They say that if her daughter does not play for the second part, the Committee will consider the contract broken and will pay nothing.

e37.description: Mrs. Kearney says angrily that she hasn't seen any Committee and that her daughter has her contract. She will get four pounds eight into her hand or a foot she won't put on that platform. Mr. Holohan says he is surprised at her and never thought she would treat them this way. Mrs. Kearney asks what way he treated her. She says she is asking for her rights and that when she asks when her daughter is going to be paid she can't get a civil answer.

e38.description: Mrs. Kearney stands at the door, haggard with rage, arguing with her husband and daughter. She waits until it is time for the second part to begin in the hope that the secretaries will approach her. But Miss Healy has kindly consented to play one or two accompaniments. Mrs. Kearney has to stand aside. When the first notes of the song strike her ear, she catches up her daughter's cloak and says to her husband 'Get a cab!' He goes out at once. Mrs. Kearney wraps the cloak round her daughter and follows him. As she passes through the doorway she stops and glares into Mr. Holohan's face and says 'I'm not done with you yet.' Mr. Holohan replies 'But I'm done with you.'

Formalist Reading: Structure, Style, and.name: Formalist Reading: Structure, Style, and Narrative Technique
Formalist Reading: Structure, Style, and.description: A formalist analysis of 'A Mother' focusing on Joyce's narrative structure, stylistic choices, symbolic patterns, and the formal construction of meaning through language, form, and compositional technique rather than biographical or historical context.

theme-form-vs-content.name: Form vs. Content Conflict
theme-form-vs-content.description: The tension between the formal structure of the contract and the informal reality of its execution; between Mrs. Kearney's rigid adherence to contractual form and the fluid, unpredictable nature of social reality.

theme-narrative-distance.name: Narrative Distance and Irony
theme-narrative-distance.description: Joyce's use of third-person limited perspective to create ironic distance between the narrator's apparent sympathy and the reader's growing awareness of Mrs. Kearney's rigidity and the futility of her position.

theme-linguistic-precision.name: Linguistic Precision and Characterization
theme-linguistic-precision.description: The use of precise, economical language to reveal character through speech patterns, physical descriptions, and narrative detail; the formal properties of language as a means of characterization.

theme-structural-parallelism.name: Structural Parallelism and Repetition
theme-structural-parallelism.description: The formal repetition of scenes, conversations, and structural patterns that create meaning through formal arrangement rather than plot development; the cyclical structure of failed negotiations.

theme-symbolic-objects.name: Objects as Formal Signifiers
theme-symbolic-objects.description: The use of material objects (contract, banknotes, charmeuse, badges) as formal elements that carry symbolic weight and structure the narrative through their presence and absence.

sym-contract.name: The Contract
sym-contract.description: A formal document that represents the tension between written form and social reality; the contract is the central formal structure around which the narrative is organized, yet its formal validity cannot guarantee its enforcement.

currentMeanings.description: Formal legal obligation and written agreement
The inadequacy of formal structures to control social reality

sym-banknotes.name: Banknotes and Payment
sym-banknotes.description: Material objects that represent the gap between formal obligation and actual fulfillment; the partial payment becomes a formal marker of the contract's breakdown and the inadequacy of form.

currentMeanings.description: Concrete evidence of obligation and exchange
The incompleteness and inadequacy of formal settlement
The material reality that resists formal arrangement

sym-concert-rooms.name: The Antient Concert Rooms
sym-concert-rooms.description: A formal architectural space that structures the narrative; the building's physical layout (vestibule, dressing-room, hall, balcony) creates the formal arrangement of scenes and the spatial organization of conflict.

currentMeanings.description: The formal space of artistic performance and social convention
The inadequacy of formal spaces to contain social conflict
The separation between public performance and private negotiation

sym-charmeuse.name: Blush-Pink Charmeuse
sym-charmeuse.description: A material object representing Mrs. Kearney's investment in formal appearance and social presentation; the fabric's delicate nature contrasts with the harsh reality of the conflict.

currentMeanings.description: Mrs. Kearney's investment in formal presentation and appearance
The fragility of social forms and aesthetic arrangements
The gap between formal preparation and actual outcome

sym-dirty-papers.name: Dirty Pieces of Paper
sym-dirty-papers.description: The informal, disorganized material basis of formal organization; Mr. Holohan's papers represent the gap between formal intention and actual execution, between the ideal form of organization and its messy reality.

currentMeanings.description: The informal, disorganized basis of formal arrangements

symrel-contract-obligation.name: Contract as Formal Obligation
symrel-contract-obligation.description: The contract symbolizes the formal structure of obligation that Mrs. Kearney insists upon; it represents the attempt to impose formal order on social reality.
symrel-contract-obligation.nature: The contract is the formal embodiment of Mrs. Kearney's belief that written form can control social reality; its failure demonstrates the inadequacy of form.
symrel-contract-obligation.interpretation: The contract is the formal embodiment of Mrs. Kearney's belief that written form can control social reality; its failure demonstrates the inadequacy of form.

symrel-payment-incompleteness.name: Partial Payment as Formal Failure
symrel-payment-incompleteness.description: The partial payment of banknotes symbolizes the breakdown of formal obligation and the inadequacy of form to ensure complete fulfillment.
symrel-payment-incompleteness.nature: The incomplete payment is a formal marker of the contract's failure; it demonstrates that form cannot guarantee substance.
symrel-payment-incompleteness.interpretation: The incomplete payment is a formal marker of the contract's failure; it demonstrates that form cannot guarantee substance.

symrel-rooms-conflict.name: Concert Rooms as Formal Container
symrel-rooms-conflict.description: The architectural space of the concert rooms becomes a formal container that cannot contain the social conflict; the physical structure mirrors the narrative structure.
symrel-rooms-conflict.nature: The concert rooms' formal structure (dressing-room, hall, balcony) creates the spatial arrangement of scenes; the conflict unfolds within this formal structure.
symrel-rooms-conflict.interpretation: The concert rooms' formal structure (dressing-room, hall, balcony) creates the spatial arrangement of scenes; the conflict unfolds within this formal structure.

symrel-charmeuse-appearance.name: Charmeuse as Formal Presentation
symrel-charmeuse-appearance.description: The blush-pink charmeuse symbolizes Mrs. Kearney's investment in formal appearance and social presentation, which contrasts with the harsh reality of the conflict.
symrel-charmeuse-appearance.nature: The delicate fabric represents the fragility of formal social arrangements; its presence in the narrative emphasizes the gap between appearance and reality.

symrel-papers-disorder.name: Dirty Papers as Organizational Failure
symrel-papers-disorder.description: The dirty pieces of paper symbolize the gap between formal intention and actual execution; they represent the disorganized reality beneath formal arrangements.

narrator.name: Third-Person Limited Narrator
narrator.description: Joyce employs a third-person limited perspective that primarily follows Mrs. Kearney's consciousness while maintaining ironic distance. The narrator presents events with apparent neutrality but through careful selection of detail, speech patterns, and physical description creates an ironic commentary on Mrs. Kearney's rigidity and the futility of her position. The narrative style is economical and precise, using free indirect discourse to blend Mrs. Kearney's thoughts with the narrator's observations.

reader.name: Implied Reader of Modernist Fiction
reader.description: The reader is positioned to initially sympathize with Mrs. Kearney's reasonable demands for contractual fulfillment, but through the narrator's ironic presentation and the accumulation of formal details, the reader gradually recognizes Mrs. Kearney's rigidity and the self-defeating nature of her position. The reader must actively interpret the formal patterns and ironic distance to construct meaning.

author.name: James Joyce
author.description: Joyce constructs this narrative with careful attention to formal properties: precise language, structural parallelism, symbolic objects, and ironic narrative distance. The story demonstrates Joyce's modernist technique of using form itself to create meaning, rather than relying on plot or character development. The narrative structure mirrors the formal conflict at its center.

e01.note: Introduces Mr. Holohan and establishes the formal organizing principle of the narrative; the 'dirty pieces of paper' symbolize the gap between formal intention and actual execution.

e02.note: Provides crucial formal characterization of Mrs. Kearney through precise physical and psychological description; establishes her 'pale and unbending manner' as a formal trait.

e03.note: Formal exposition of Mrs. Kearney's marriage; the phrase 'out of spite' introduces the theme of form constraining desire.

e04.note: Establishes Mr. Kearney's character through formal enumeration of his virtues; the list structure emphasizes formal organization.

e05.note: Minor formal detail establishing Mrs. Kearney's social performance; the repetition of 'every year' emphasizes formal patterns.
